verses.zh: 耶稣抬头观看，见财主把捐项投在库里，
verses.en: Jesus[NOTE:1] looked up[NOTE:2] and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “He”; the referent has been specified in the translation for clarity. Here δέ (de) has not been translated.
Grk “looking up, he saw.” The participle ἀναβλέψας (anablepsas) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

The offering box probably refers to the receptacles in the temple forecourt by the Court of Women used to collect freewill offerings. These are mentioned by Josephus, J. W. 5.5.2 (5.200), 6.5.2 (6.282); Ant. 19.6.1 (19.294); and in 1 Macc 14:49 and 2 Macc 3:6, 24, 28, 40 (see also Mark 12:41; John 8:20).tn On the term γαζοφυλάκιον (gazophulakion), often translated “treasury,” see BDAG 186 s.v., which states, “For Mk 12:41, 43; Lk 21:1 the mng. contribution box or receptacle is attractive. Acc. to Mishnah, Shekalim 6, 5 there were in the temple 13 such receptacles in the form of trumpets. But even in these passages the general sense of ‘treasury’ is prob., for the contributions would go [into] the treasury via the receptacles.” Based upon the extra-biblical evidence (see sn following), however, the translation opts to refer to the actual receptacles and not the treasury itself.
verses.commentary:
21:1-4 This is paralleled in Mark 12:41-44.

21:1 "the treasury" This is a compound word of "treasure" and "guard" (cf. LXX 2 Kgs. 23:11; Esth. 3:9;
Ezra 5:17; 6:1; 7:20). Jewish tradition (Shekalim 6 [fourth tractate in Mo’ed]; Josephus,
Jewish Wars 5.5.2; 6.5.2; Antiq. 19.6.2; and Alfred Edersheim, Temple, pp. 48-49) asserts
that there were thirteen trumpet-shaped, metal boxes located in the Court of the Women, where Jesus regularly
taught (cf. Luke 20:1). Each one of them was designated for a different charitable purpose (cf. John 8:20).
Archaeology has never confirmed the existence of these metal containers.

verses.zh: 又见一个穷寡妇投了两个小钱，
verses.en: He also saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins.[NOTE:1]
notes: These two small copper coins were lepta (sing. “lepton”), the smallest and least valuable coins in circulation in Palestine, worth one-half of a quadrans or 1/128 of a denarius, or about six minutes of an average daily wage. This was next to nothing in value.
verses.commentary:
21:2 "a poor widow" Luke chooses from Jesus' words and actions to cast the religious and social outcasts
of His day in a positive light (esp. women). Here a poor widow set the standard of sacrificial giving that all
disciples should emulate.

▣ "two small copper coins" This refers to two copper Jewish coins called lepton. This term
means "the thin one." This is the only Jewish coin mentioned in the NT. Two lepta equal one quadrant;
four quadrants equal one assarion; 16 assarions equal one denarius, which was a
day's wage for a soldier or laborer.

Commentators often mentioned that someone could not give one lepta (rabbinical tradition),
but this is a misunderstanding of the Jewish Talmud.

Special Topic: Coins Used in Palestine in Jesus' Day

verses.zh: 就说：「我实在告诉你们，这穷寡妇所投的比众人还多；
verses.en: He[NOTE:1] said, “I tell you the truth,[NOTE:2] this poor widow has put in more than all of them.[NOTE:3]
notes: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “Truly, I say to you.”
Has put in more than all of them. With God, giving is weighed evaluatively, not counted. The widow was praised because she gave sincerely and at some considerable cost to herself.
verses.commentary:
21:3 "Truly" This is the Greek term alēthōs (cf. Luke 9:27; 12:44), which is used
synonymously with amēn in Luke 21:32. The parallel in Mark 12:43 has amēn.

Special Topic: Amen

verses.zh: 因为众人都是自己有余，拿出来投在捐项里，但这寡妇是自己不足，把她一切养生的都投上了。」
verses.en: For they all offered their gifts out of their wealth.[NOTE:1] But she, out of her poverty, put in everything she had to live on.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “out of what abounded to them.”
Or “put in her entire livelihood.”

21:4

Literally this is "put into the gifts" (cf. MSS א, B, and L),
but several other uncial manuscripts (cf. MSS A, D, W) and most ancient versions add "of God" to clarify the
context for Gentiles. The UBS4 committee rated the shorter text as "B" (almost certain).

▣ "out of their surplus" This same principle of spiritual giving is found in 2 Cor. 8:12. It is
surprising that the NT does not discuss regular giving principles. 2 Corinthians 8-9 deals with the Gentile
churches' one-time gift to the mother church in Jerusalem. Tithing is an OT principle.

Special Topic: Tithing

▣ "put in all that she had to live on" This woman trusted in God's daily provision (cf. Matt. 6:33).
Luke records many of Jesus' teachings about worldly possessions and wealth. Giving is a spiritual thermometer. It
reveals our motives and priorities.

But please rememeber that much of Jesus' teachings are hyperbolic for impact. Believers must
also provide for their families (cf. 1 Tim. 5:8).

Special Topic: Wealth

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS FOR JESUS' OLIVET DISCOURSE

- Matthew records several long sermons/teaching sessions of Jesus. They seem to be made up of

- Jesus' repeated emphases in different locations, with different audiences

- Matthew combining these to form long sermons. Matthew's Olivet discourse is three times
longer than Mark 13 or Luke 21.

- a good example of this is Matt. 24, where Matthew adds Jesus' discussion

- Matt. 24:36-44 is found only in Luke 17:22-37

- Matt. 24:45-51 is not in the parallels. Each Gospel writer had his own sources.

- Matthew 24, Mark 13, and Luke 21 are so difficult to interpret because they deal with either two or three questions
simultaneously (cf. Matt. 24:3).

- When will the temple be destroyed? (the questions in Mark and Luke)

- What will be the sign of the Messiah's return?

- for the judgment on the temple (i.e., Hebrew idiom, "coming")

- the Second Coming (but at this point the disciples would have no knowledge of this event)

- When will this age end?

- the age of temple law

- end time

Special Topic: Disciples' Questions

- The genre of New Testament eschatological passages is usually a combination of apocalyptic and
prophetic language, which is purposely ambiguous and highly symbolic. One must be familiar with the OT to understand
the imagery being used. See

- D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptics

- Fee and Stuart, How To Read the Bible For All Its Worth, pp. 181-204

- C. B. Caird, The Langauge and Imagery of the Bible

Special Topic: Apocalyptic Literature

Special Topic: Prophecy (OT)

- Several passages in the NT (cf. Matthew 24, Mark 13, Luke 17 and 21, 1 and 2 Thessalonians
and Revelation) deal with a temporal divine coming in judgment, as does the OT. These passages emphasize

- the exact time of the event is unknown but the event is certain (i.e., Matt. 24:36)

- we can know the general time but not the specific time of the events (i.e., Matt. 24:32)

- it will occur suddenly and unexpectedly (i.e., Matt. 24:43)

- we must be prayerful, ready, and faithful to assigned tasks (i.e., Matt. 24:42,44)

Many scholars see Matt. 24 parallel with Rev. 6. It is John's way of recording the Olivet Discourse.

- There is a theological paradoxical tension between

- the any-moment return (cf. Matt. 24:27,44)

- the fact that some events in history must occur

Special Topic: The Any-Moment Return of Jesus vs. The Not Yet

Special Topic: Delayed Second Coming

- The New Testament states that some events will occur before the temporal divine judgment on apostate
Judaism (i.e., A.D. 66-70):

- The gospel preached to the known world (cf. Matt. 24:14; Mark 13:10)

- The great Jewish apostasy (cf. Matt. 24:10-13, 21; 1 Tim. 4:1; 2 Tim. 3:1ff.; 2 Thess. 2:3)

- The revelation of the "man of lawlessness" (cf. Dan. 7:23-26; 9:24-27; 2 Thess. 2:3)

- Removal of that/who restrains (cf. 2 Thess. 2:6-7)

- For good resources on comparing the different theories related to this chapter, see

- Four views On the Book of Revelation several authors (ISBN 0-310-21080-1)

- Preterism ‒ pp. 35-92

- Idealism ᰪ pp. 93-132

- Progressive Dispensationalism ‒ pp. 133-176

- Classical Dispensationalsim ‒ pp. 177-231

verses.zh: 有人谈论圣殿是用美石和供物妆饰的；
verses.en: Now[NOTE:1] while some were speaking about the temple, how it was adorned[NOTE:2] with beautiful stones and offerings,[NOTE:3] Jesus[NOTE:4] said,
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “now” to indicate the transition to a new topic.

The Jerusalem temple was widely admired around the world. See Josephus, Ant. 15.11 (15.380-425); J. W. 5.5 (5.184-227) and Tacitus, History 5.8, who called it “immensely opulent.” Josephus compared it to a beautiful snowcapped mountain.
For the translation of ἀνάθημα (anathēma) as “offering” see L&N 53.18.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
21:5 "And while some were talking about the temple" In Mark 13 (and Matthew 24) it is the inner circle of
disciples who mention the beautiful temple building as they walked from the upper room through the temple Court
of the Gentiles toward the Mount of Olives. But Luke puts the discussion of the beauty of Herod's Temple in the
Court of the Women in the temple itself. Herod's temple was not completely finished until A.D. 63,
seven years before it was destroyed by Titus' army. This remodeled and enlarged national shrine was the
object of Jewish religion (cf. Jeremiah 7).

The differences between the Synoptic Gospels cause many to doubt the historicity of the three (often)
different accounts.

- First, it must be remembered the Gospels are not cause-and-effect, western, chronological histories. They are
gospel tracts targeting different communities/cultures. Luke, like John, is written to Gentiles.

- The Gospel writers under inspiration had the right to

- choose some of Jesus' acts and teachings (but not all, cf. John 20:30-31; 21:25)

- rearrange to chronological order Jesus' words and actions (i.e., cleaning of the temple, early in John,
the last week of Jesus' life in the Synoptics)

- adapt the words and actions to fit the Gospel writer's overall theme (i.e., this is not to imply they could make
things up)

- For a good discussion of the literary genre of the Gospels, see Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, How To
Read the Bible For All Its Worth, the chapter on the Gospels

▣ "adorned stones" Herod's temple was built with huge polished limestones (i.e., mezzeh),
which were 25 x 8 x 12 cubits (a cubit is 18-21"). Josephus records this information in Antiq. 15.11.3. It was one of
the wonders of the ancient world (Tacitus, History 5.8)

Special Topic: Cubit

This is the Greek term anathēma, which is used only here in the NT. In the
Septuagint it can refer to

- a votive offering (cf. II Macc. 9:16)

- an accursed thing (i.e., something given to God and thereby becomes holy and cannot be used by
human beings, cf. Deut. 7:26)

One example of this was Herod's lavish gift of a huge golden grapevine that hung at the entrance
of the Holy Place. The grapes were as tall as a man (cf. Josephus, Antiq. 15.2.3). This grapevine was a
symbol of national Israel (cf. Ps. 80:8; Isa. 5:1-7).

Special Topic: Curse

verses.zh: 耶稣就说：「论到你们所看见的这一切，将来日子到了，在这里没有一块石头留在石头上，不被拆毁了。」
verses.en: “As for these things that you are gazing at, the days will come when not one stone will be left on another.[NOTE:1] All will be torn down!”[NOTE:2]
notes: With the statement days will come when not one stone will be left on another Jesus predicted the total destruction of the temple, something that did occur in a.d. 70.
Grk “the days will come when not one stone will be left on another that will not be thrown down.”
verses.commentary:
21:6 "there will not be left one stone upon another which will not be torn down" This is imagery of
total destruction. It exactly describes the Roman destruction of Jerusalem under Titus
in A.D. 70 (i.e., according to Josephus, Jewish Wars). The only stones left were the foundation
stones of Solomon's temple that are today known as the "Wailing Wall." This total destruction was prophesied in
Micah 3:12 and Jer. 26:18.

This destruction is described in detail beginning in A.D. 66 in Galilee by Vespasian and
finished by Titus' siege and dismantling of Jerusalem and the temple. This was God's judgment on "those who pierced
Him" (cf. Rev. 1:7). I have come to understand that most of Jesus' Olivet Discourse and the book of Revelation predict
and describe this event. This theological understanding is called Partial Preterism.

If you are interested in the historical and textual basis of this interpretive opinion, see

- John Bray, Matthew 24 fulfilled

- Kenneth Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell

- Steve Gregg, Revelation: Four Views, Revised and Updated

verses.zh: 他们问他说：「夫子！甚么时候有这事呢？这事将到的时候有甚么预兆呢？」
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] they asked him,[NOTE:2] “Teacher, when will these things[NOTE:3] happen? And what will be the sign that[NOTE:4] these things are about to take place?”
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of Jesus’ comments about the temple’s future destruction.
Grk “asked him, saying.” The participle λέγοντες (legontes) is redundant in English and has not been translated.
Both references to these things are plural, so more than the temple’s destruction is in view. The question may presuppose that such a catastrophe signals the end.
Grk “when.”
verses.commentary:
21:7 "They questioned Him" From Mark 13:3 we know that "they" refers to Peter, James, John, and Andrew.
They seem to have asked two or three questions.

- when will the temple be destroyed

- what will be the sign of the coming destruction

- when will this age end and the new age begin (recorded only in Matt. 24:3)

Special Topic: The Disciples' Questions

verses.zh: 耶稣说：「你们要谨慎，不要受迷惑；因为将来有好些人冒我的名来，说：『我是基督』，又说：『时候近了』，你们不要跟从他们！
verses.en: He[NOTE:1] said, “Watch out[NOTE:2] that you are not misled. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’[NOTE:3] and, ‘The time is near.’ Do not follow them!
notes: Here δέ (de) has not been translated.
Or “Be on guard.”
That is, “I am the Messiah.”
verses.commentary:
21:8 "See to it that you are not misled" This is a PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVE and
an AORIST PASSIVE SUBJUNCTIVE. It refers to the many Messianic pretenders active in the city
of Jerusalem during the Roman siege (A.D. 69-70. It was this nationalistic religious fanaticism that
led to the total destruction of Jerusalem (cf. Josephus, Wars of the Jews 6.54).

▣ "misled" This is the Greek VERB planaō, from which the English
word "planet" (i.e., the wanderers) is derived. It refers to the unusual orbit of the planets compared
to the constellations (stars). It is usually translated "error," but came to be used as imagery for deceiving
or leading astray (cf. Matt. 24:4,5,11,24; also note Luke 17:23).

▣ "'I am He'" This reflects Jesus' use of the OT covenant name for God, YHWH (cf. Exod. 3:14)
as a designation of Himself (cf. John 8:24,58; 13:19; 18:5). Here it means many false prophets would claim to
be the Jewish Messiah of Deut. 18:18-19 (cf. Acts 3:20-23).

Special Topic: Names for Deity, D.

▣ "The time is near" This phrase in this context is the message of the pseudo-Messiahs. This is another
example of the delayed Second Coming emphasis in Luke. This refers to the time period between Jesus' ministry and the destruction
of Jerusalem. The other Gospels and Revelation use this phrase as a time indicator by Jesus.

Special Topic: Temporal Markers in the Olivet Discourse

▣ "do not go after them" This is an AORIST PASSIVE (deponent) SUBJUNCTIVE
used in the sense of an IMPERATIVE (Mark 13:7 is a PRESENT IMPERATIVE). It has
the NEGATIVE PARTICLE, which usually denotes stopping an act in progress. These false messiahs
had a large and zealous following. Nationalism is a tricky master. It tends to pull us away from the priority of the Kingdom
of God.

verses.zh: 你们听见打仗和扰乱的事，不要惊惶；因为这些事必须先有，只是末期不能立时就到。」
verses.en: And when you hear of wars and rebellions,[NOTE:1] do not be afraid.[NOTE:2] For these things must happen first, but the end will not come at once.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Social and political chaos also precedes the end. This term refers to revolutions (L&N 39.34).
This is not the usual term for fear, but refers to a deep sense of terror and emotional distress (Luke 24:37; BDAG 895 s.v. πτοέω).
The end will not come at once. This remark about timing not only indicates that there will be events before the end, but that some time will also pass before it comes.
verses.commentary:
21:9-11 These are precursor signs that are observable in every age (cf. Mark 13:7-8; Matt. 24:6-8). They designate
the kind of world we live in, not uniquely the world immediately before the coming of Jesus Christ in judgment on "those who
pierced Him" (cf. Rev. 1:7, cf. John L. Bray, Matthew 24 Fulfilled, pp. 25,28).

21:9 "do not be terrified" This is another AORIST PASSIVE SUBJUNCTIVE used in the sense of
an IMPERATIVE. It is also an idiom from the Septuagint. The times of temporal judgment nor the eschatological
judgment should frighten believers because their sins have been forgiven and they are fully accepted by God in Christ!

Special Topic: Septuagint

verses.zh: 当时，耶稣对他们说：「民要攻打民，国要攻打国；
verses.en: Then he said to them, “Nation will rise up in arms[NOTE:1] against nation, and kingdom against kingdom.
notes: For the translation “rise up in arms” see L&N 55.2.
verses.commentary:
21:10 "these things must take place first" The Markan parallel calls these precursor events "the beginning
of the birth pangs of the new age" (cf. Mark 13:7-8). Both Mark and Luke have the word dei (must),
which means necessity. God's children need to know and trust that all things are working out according to
His plan!

Special Topic: Birth Pains of the New Age

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

verses.zh: 地要大大震动，多处必有饥荒、瘟疫，又有可怕的异象和大神迹从天上显现。
verses.en: There will be great earthquakes, and famines[NOTE:1] and plagues in various places, and there will be terrifying sights[NOTE:2] and great signs[NOTE:3] from heaven.
notes: This term, φόβητρον (phobētron), occurs only here in the NT. It could refer to an object, event, or condition that causes fear, but in the context it is linked with great signs from heaven, so the translation “sights” was preferred.

Special Topic: The Second Coming, IV.)

▣ "great signs from heaven" The author uses OT apocalyptic language to describe these events
(cf. Mark 13:25). Peter says that the prophecy of Joel 2:28-32, which also uses apocalyptic language, was
fulfilled at Pentecost (cf. Acts 2), which shows it was not meant to be understood literally. Two books that have
really helped me to better understand prophecy and apocalyptic literature are:

- D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares & Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic

- Gary DeMar, Last Days Madness, pp. 131-157

There are several slightly different versions of the phrase in the Greek manuscript tradition.
The variations do not alter the sense of the phrase in context. There is no way to determine which of the
five Greek MSS variants is original.

Special Topic: Sign (OT)

verses.zh: 但这一切的事以先，人要下手拿住你们，逼迫你们，把你们交给会堂，并且收在监里，又为我的名拉你们到君王诸侯面前。
verses.en: But before all this,[NOTE:1] they will seize[NOTE:2] you and persecute you, handing you over to the synagogues[NOTE:3] and prisons. You[NOTE:4] will be brought before kings and governors because of my name.
notes: But before all this. Another note of timing is present, this one especially important in understanding the sequence in the discourse. Before the things noted in vv. 8-11 are the events of vv. 12-19.
Grk “will lay their hands on you.”
Some of the persecution is of Jewish origin (the synagogues). Some fulfillment of this can be seen in Acts. See the note on synagogues in 4:15.
Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was started here in the translation.
verses.commentary:
21:12 There have been many examples both in Acts and in church history of this kind of persecution of
believers. Notice the different types of persecution (i.e., "lay hands on," a LXX idiom).

- synagogues ‒ beatings for violation of Mosaic Law or judicial decision
(cf. Deut. 25:1-3; Matt. 19:17; 23:34; Mark 13:9; Acts 6:9-10; see Contextual Insights, A. from Mark 13)

- local governmental authorities (i.e., the different sons of Herod)

- Roman authorities (Proconsuls or Procurators)

- regional (governors)

- in Rome (kings)

The NASB Study Bible (footnote Luke 21:12, p. 1503) asserts that the synagogue was also used as a
place of confinement until trial.

This Jesiwh and Roman persecution of believers related to the historical period before A.D.
70. Jews lost all influence and political power after the Jewish War (A.D. 66-70). This is one reason I
think a Partial Preterism fits the Olivet Discourse and the book of Revelation best.

The reason it is titled "Partial Preterism" is because the Second Coming of Jesus is predicted and
promised in so many texts ‒ Acts 1:11; 3:19-21; 1 Cor. 1:7; 15:23; Phi. 3:20-21; 1 Thess. 2:19; 3:3; 4:13-18; 5:23;
2 Thess. 1:7,10; 1 Tim. 6:14; 2 Tim. 4:1,8; Titus 2:13; Heb. 9:28; James 5:7-9; 1 Pet. 1:7,13; 2 Pet. 1:16; 3:8-13; 1 John 2:28.

Special Topic: The Second Coming

verses.zh: 但这些事终必为你们的见证。
verses.en: This will be a time for you to serve as witnesses.[NOTE:1]
notes: Grk “This will turn out to you for [a] testimony.”
verses.commentary:
21:13 Persecution can lead to proclamation opportunities (e.g., Paul in prison in Rome). It is surprising
that Luke does not retain Mark's wording at this point because it fits Luke's purpose in writing his Gospel
so well (i.e., Mark 13:10, "and the Gospel must be preached to all the nations")!

Special Topic: Why Do Christians Suffer?

verses.zh: 所以，你们当立定心意，不要预先思想怎样分诉；
verses.en: Therefore be resolved[NOTE:1] not to rehearse[NOTE:2] ahead of time how to make your defense.
notes: Grk “determine in your hearts.”
This term could refer to rehearsing a speech or a dance. On its syntax, see BDF §392.2.
verses.commentary:
21:14-15 This text does not refer to regular sermon preparation and Bible lessons (usually quoted by lazy
preachers and teachers), but to specific testimony in the face of persecution and trials before Jewish authorities (cf. Acts 7)
or governmental authorities (cf. Luke 12:11-12).

verses.zh: 因为我必赐你们口才、智慧，是你们一切敌人所敌不住、驳不倒的。
verses.en: For I will give you the words[NOTE:1] along with the wisdom[NOTE:2] that none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict.
notes: Grk “a mouth.” It is a metonymy and refers to the reply the Lord will give to them.
Grk “and wisdom.”

verses.zh: 连你们的父母、弟兄、亲族、朋友也要把你们交官；你们也有被他们害死的。
verses.en: You will be betrayed even by parents,[NOTE:1] brothers, relatives,[NOTE:2] and friends, and they will have some of you put to death.
notes: To confess Christ might well mean rejection by one’s own family, even by parents.

Grk “and brothers and relatives,” but καί (kai) has not been translated twice here since English normally uses a coordinating conjunction only between the last two elements in a series of three or more.
verses.commentary:
21:16 "you will be betrayed even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends" Faith in Christ will
divide families and lifelong friends (cf. Matt. 10:21; Mark 13:12). This may be what Matt. 24:40-41 means.

verses.zh: 你们要为我的名被众人恨恶，
verses.en: You will be hated by everyone because of my name.[NOTE:1]
verses.commentary:
21:17 "you will be hated by all because of My name" This is a PERIPHRASTIC FUTURE PASSIVE. The
presence of "all" shows it is a hyperbole (exaggeration). Christians will be hated because of their identification
with Jesus of Nazareth (cf. Luke 6:22; John 9:22; 15:19; 16:2; 17:14,16; 1 Pet. 4:12-16). The early church was accused of

- atheism (no visible God)

- treason (would not join Roman's military)

- incest (they loved one another)

- cannibalism (misunderstanding of Lord's Supper, John 6)

which were all related to a misunderstanding of Christian doctrines, terminologies, and worship
procedures. Persecution for Christ's sake is a NT evidence of believer's salvation and effective Christian living
(cf. John 8:47; 18:37; 1 John 4:5-6).

Special Topic: The Name of the Lord

verses.zh: 然而，你们连一根头发也必不损坏。
verses.en: Yet[NOTE:1] not a hair of your head will perish.[NOTE:2]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “yet” to indicate the contrast present in this context.
Given v. 16, the expression not a hair of your head will perish must be taken figuratively and refer to living ultimately in the presence of God.
verses.commentary:
21:18 "Yet not a hair of your head will perish" This is a strong DOUBLE NEGATIVE. Verse 18
seems to contradict Luke 21:16. However, it must be understood that the main thrust here is

- God is in control of history

- physical death is not ultimate for believers

Jesus used this same OT idiom of protection (cf. 1 Sam. 14:45; 2 Sam. 14:11; 1 Kgs. 1:52) in
previous sermons (cf. Luke 12:7; Matt. 10:30). Thank God for Romans 8:31-39!

▣ "perish" This is the Greek term apollumi.

Robert B. Girdlestone, Synonyms of the Old Testament, p. 276, points out that there are
several places where this term cannot be translated annihilation, "but such injury as makes the object practically
useless for its original purpose."

- the waste of ointment, Matt. 26:8

- destruction of old wine skins, Matt. 9:17

- destruction of hair, Luke 21:18

- destruction of food, John 6:27

- destruction of gold, 1 Pet. 1:7

- destruction of the world, 2 Peter. 3:6

- destruction of the physical body, Matt. 2:13; 8:25; 12:14; 21:41; 22:7; 26:52; 27:20; Rom. 2:12; 14:15;
and 1 Cor. 8:11

This refers to the end of bodily existence. It is also
commonly used in a moral sense. "All men are regarded as morally destroyed, i.e., they have failed to carry out
the intention for which the race was called into being" (p. 276). God's response to this problem was Jesus
Christ (cf. John 3:15-16 and 2 Pet. 3:9). Those who reject the gospel are now subject to a further destruction,
which does involve body and spirit (cf. 1 Cor. 1:18; 2 Cor. 2:15; 4:3; 2 Thess. 2:10).

I have come to believe in "limited immortality." Only God is ever living and those He chooses to give
eternal life (i.e., believers in Jesus). This has caused me to rethink "eternal conscious torment." I hope you will look
at the YouTube videos by

- Edward William Fudge, The Fire That Consumes: A Biblical and Historical Study of the
Doctrine of Final Punishment (video and book)
YouTube One Hour Lecture

- Steve Gregg, "Hell: Three Views" (video)

verses.zh: 你们常存忍耐，就必保全灵魂（或译：必得生命）。」
verses.en: By your endurance[NOTE:1] you will gain[NOTE:2] your lives.[NOTE:3]
notes: By your endurance is a call to remain faithful because trusting in Jesus is the means to life.

Some significant Greek witnesses plus the majority of mss (א D L W Ψ ƒ1 M) read the aorist imperative κτήσασθε (ktēsasthe) here, though some mss (A B Θ ƒ13 33 lat sa) read the future indicative κτήσεσθε (ktēsesthe). A decision is difficult because the evidence is so evenly balanced, but the aorist imperative is the harder reading and better explains the rise of the other. J. A. Fitzmyer assesses the translation options this way: “In English one has to use something similar [i.e., a future indicative], even if one follows the [aorist imperative]” (Luke [AB], 2:1341); in the same vein, although this translation follows the aorist imperative because of English requirements it has been translated as though it were a future indicative.

Grk “your souls,” but ψυχή (psuchē) is frequently used of one’s physical life. In light of v. 16 that does not seem to be the case here. The entire phrase could be taken as an idiom meaning “you will save yourselves” (L&N 21.20), or (as in v. 18) this could refer to living ultimately in the presence of God.
verses.commentary:
21:19 This same emphasis on perseverance is found in Matt. 10:22; 24:13; Rom. 2:7; 5:3-4; Heb. 10:36.
True faith is a faith that lasts!

There is a Greek manuscript variant in the VERB.

- AORIST MIDDLE (deponent) IMPERATIVE (cf. MSS
א, D. L, W)

- FUTURE MIDDLE INDICATIVE (cf. MSS A, B, and most ancient versions)

The UBS4 chooses #1, but "with difficulty" ("C" rating). The UBS3 gave #1 a
D rating, "with great difficulty."

▣ "you will gain your lives" This is the Greek word psuchē (souls), which reflects the Hebrew
word nephesh (BDB 659, i.e., physical life). Because of verse 16 this must refer to one's spiritual
life. Christians will be killed but they have eternal life (cf. Matt. 10:28). See the word play between the
two meanings at Mark 8:35-37.

verses.zh: 「你们看见耶路撒冷被兵围困，就可知道它成荒场的日子近了。
verses.en: “But when you see Jerusalem[NOTE:1] surrounded[NOTE:2] by armies, then know that its[NOTE:3] desolation[NOTE:4] has come near.
notes: For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
See Luke 19:41-44. This passage refers to the events associated with the fall of Jerusalem, when the city is surrounded by armies.
Grk “her,” referring to the city of Jerusalem (the name “Jerusalem” in Greek is a feminine noun).

The phrase its desolation is a reference to the fall of the city, which is the only antecedent present in Luke’s account. The parallels to this in Matt 24:15 and Mark 13:14 refer to the temple’s desolation, though Matthew’s allusion is clearer. They focus on the parallel events of the end, not on the short term realization in a.d. 70. The entire passage has a prophetic “two events in one” typology, where the near term destruction (a.d. 70) is like the end. So the evangelists could choose to focus on the near time realization (Luke) or on its long term fulfillment, which mirrors it (Matthew, Mark).
verses.commentary:
21:20 "when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies" Vespasian was Nero's general who subdued Palestine,
(A.D. 66-68) but at Nero's suicide (A.D. 68) he had to return to Rome (A.D. 69) where
three Emperors (Galba, Ortho, and Vitrello) followed in less than one year. Finally, Vespasian became Emperor and his son, Titus, destroyed
the city and the temple in A.D. 70 after a five month siege of Jerusalem (cf. Luke 19:43) beginning in April when the city was flooded
with pilgrims. Josephus vividly describes this period in his Jewish Wars (see Kenneth Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell).

The parallels in the Synoptic Gospels (i.e., Matt. 24:15 and Mark 13:14) mention
"the abomination of desolation" (see Special Topic:
Abomination of Desolation). Luke clarifies this as the Roman legions under Titus, Vespasian's son,
which had started a five month siege of Jerusalem. The city and temple were completely destroyed in
A.D. 70.

For a good indepth history of this period, see the YouTube videos by Bruce Gore, "The Apocalypse in Space
and Time" (10 lessons).

notes: Fleeing to the mountains is a key OT image: Gen 19:17; Judg 6:2; Isa 15:5; Jer 16:16; Zech 14:5.
Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
verses.commentary:
21:21 "Then those who are in Judea must flee to the mountains" This is a PRESENT ACTIVE
IMPERATIVE. Tradition (Eusebius, Eccl. His. 3.5.2-3) asserts that when the Christians saw the
Roman armies coming, they heeded Jesus' prophetic message and fled to the Trans-Jordan region of the Decapolis
to a city named Pella and almost all of them were spared the horrors of the siege and destruction of Jerusalem. Judaism
(i.e., the Mosaic system) was once and for all destroyed, but Christianity became a universal faith option.

verses.zh: 因为这是报应的日子，使经上所写的都得应验。
verses.en: because these are days of vengeance,[NOTE:1] to fulfill[NOTE:2] all that is written.
notes: Or “of punishment.” This is a time of judgment.
The passive construction with the infinitive πλησθῆναι (plēsthēnai) has been translated as an active construction for simplicity, in keeping with contemporary English style.
verses.commentary:
21:22 "because these are the days of vengeance" God used the Roman army to bring temporal judgment on
apostate Judaism (i.e., "those who pierced Him," cf. Rev. 1:7). This refers to the consequences of the Jewish War
(A.D. 66-70). Hundreds of thousands were killed and the rest sold into slavery (see note at v. 24). See John Bray,
Matthew 24 Fulfilled and Four Views On the Book of Revelation, pp. 35-92 and
Special Topic: The Second Comine, IV.

The Gospel of Luke records many of Jesus' teachings about the judgment of God that will fall

verses.zh: 当那些日子，怀孕的和奶孩子的有祸了！因为将有大灾难降在这地方，也有震怒临到这百姓。
verses.en: Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing their babies in those days! For there will be great distress[NOTE:1] on the earth and wrath against this people.
notes: Great distress means that this is a period of great judgment.
verses.commentary:
21:23 This obviously refers to the destruction of Jerusalem only, not to the Second Coming. The problem
was the rapid flight that was necessary (cf. Matt. 24:15-31; Mark 13:14-27).

Jesus answers the questions of the disciples. Notice also the synonymous parallelism which is so
common in OT wisdom literature. Verses 23 and 24a form three double parallel lines.

verses.zh: 他们要倒在刀下，又被掳到各国去。耶路撒冷要被外邦人践踏，直到外邦人的日期满了。」
verses.en: They[NOTE:1] will fall by the edge[NOTE:2] of the sword and be led away as captives[NOTE:3] among all nations. Jerusalem[NOTE:4] will be trampled down by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.[NOTE:5]
notes: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “by the mouth of the sword” (an idiom for the edge of a sword).
Here is the predicted judgment against the nation until the time of Gentile rule has passed: Its people will be led away as captives.
Grk “And Jerusalem.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled implies a time when Israel again has a central role in God’s plan.
verses.commentary:
21:24 "and they will fall by the edge of the sword" Verse 24 reflects Revelation 11. Josephus tells us that
1,100,000 were killed and 97,000 were taken prisoner (Wars of the Jews, 6.9.3). Josephus often exaggerated his
numbers, but the terror and horror of this event is accurate. See Gary DeMar, Last Days Madness, pp. 117-130.

▣ "and will be led captive into all the nations" The captured Jews were sold as slaves throughout
the Roman Empire (as were all defeated peoples). Two-thirds of the population of the Roman Empire were slaves.

▣ "until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled" There are several theories related to this phrase
(cf. Luke 20:16; Mark 13:10; Rom. 11:12,25).

- Gentiles as God's instrument of judgment on Israel (i.e., Dan. 8:13)

- the Gentiles in political control of Palestine (i.e., Daniel 2; Rev. 11:2b)

- the believing Gentiles receiving Israel's OT blessing and mandate of evangelism (i.e., Rom.2:28-29; Gal. 6:16;
Eph. 2:11-3:13; 1 Pet. 2:5,9; Rev. 1:6)

- the Good News being preached even to the Gentiles (i.e., Rom. 1:8; 11:25; Col. 1:6,23)

verses.zh: 「日、月、星辰要显出异兆，地上的邦国也有困苦；因海中波浪的响声，就慌慌不定。
verses.en: “And there will be signs in the sun and moon and stars,[NOTE:1] and on the earth nations will be in distress,[NOTE:2] anxious[NOTE:3] over the roaring of the sea and the surging waves.
notes: Signs in the sun and moon and stars are cosmic signs that turn our attention to the end and the Son of Man’s return for the righteous. OT imagery is present: See Isa 13:9-10; 24:18-20; 34:4; Ezek 32:7-8; Joel 2:1, 30-31; 3:15.
Grk “distress of nations.”
Or “in consternation” (L&N 32.9).
verses.commentary:
21:25-26 "There will be signs in sun and moon and stars" Again this is an example of OT apocalyptic
language concerning God's breaking into history. Because of Peter's use of Joel 2:28-32 in Acts 2, this should
not be taken literally. See note at verse 11 and Gary DeMar, Last Days Madness, pp. 131-156.

Special Topic: Apocalyptic Literature

21:25 "and on the earth dismay among nations, in perplexity at the roaring of the sea and the waves"
Apocalyptic literature has much in common with OT wisdom literature. In this text there is a good example of
synonymous parallelism. The imagery of the sea for the nations comes from Daniel (cf. Dan. 7:2-3).

Special Topic: Wisdom Literature

verses.zh: 天势都要震动，人想起那将要临到世界的事，就都吓得魂不附体。
verses.en: People will be fainting from fear[NOTE:1] and from the expectation of what is coming on the world, for the powers of the heavens will be shaken.[NOTE:2]
notes: According to L&N 23.184 this could be mainly a psychological experience rather than actual loss of consciousness. It could also refer to complete discouragement because of fear, leading people to give up hope (L&N 25.293).

An allusion to Isa 34:4. The heavens were seen as the abode of heavenly forces, so their shaking indicates distress in the spiritual realm. Although some take the powers as a reference to bodies in the heavens (like stars and planets, “the heavenly bodies,” NIV) this is not as likely.
verses.commentary:
21:26 "coming upon the world" This phrase is unique to Luke. It refers to the known inhabited world,
not the whole planet. It may refer to the chaos in Rome with the suicide of Nero in A.D. 68.

▣ "for the powers of the heavens will be shaken" This reflects several passages in Isa. 13:10,13;
24:22; 34:4; 51:6. This imagery has two orientations.

- If this were an astral deities context it would refer to their weakness and judgment.

- If this were a visitation of YHWH context (and it is) then it refers to creation's convulsions at
the approach of its Creator.

Special Topic: Lord of Hosts

verses.zh: 那时，他们要看见人子有能力，有大荣耀驾云降临。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] they will see the Son of Man arriving in a cloud[NOTE:2] with power and great glory.
notes: Grk “And then” (καὶ τότε, kai tote). Here καί has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
An allusion to Dan 7:13. Here is Jesus returning with full judging authority.
verses.commentary:
21:27 "Then they will see" This could refer to

- all mankind

- more possibly Jews trapped in Jerusalem by Titus' siege (A.D. 69-70)

This seems to preclude a secret rapture. The concept of a secret rapture was unknown in the
church before John Darby (A.D. 1800-1882), an Anglican minister in England. His unique
theological emphasis speculated

- all OT prophecy has to be literally fulfilled to the nation of Israel

- the church is a parenthesis because the Jews rejected Jesus as the Christ (i.e., between the 69th and
70th week of Dan. 9:24-27)

- the church must be raptured out of this world so that the OT prophecies can be fulfilled to Israel during the millennium

For a good critique of this new eschatological system, please view Steve Gregg's
YouTube videos on Dispensationalism.
YouTube Lecture
- 1:34:57 He was once a teacher of this view but has changed. He, therefore, understands it
well and knows its weaknesses!

▣ "the Son of Man coming in a cloud" "Son of Man" is Jesus' self-chosen
title. It apparently comes from Ezek. 2:1 and Dan. 7:13, where it combines humanity and Deity (cf. 1 John 4:1-3). The presence of a
cloud fits OT and NT allusions to a cloud being the transportation of Deity. It is present at many of the major events
of judgment (cf. Matt. 24:30; 26:64; 1 Thess. 4:17; Rev. 1:7). See David Chilton, The Great Tribulation, pp. 16-28.

notes: These things are all the events of vv. 8-27. Disciples represent the righteous here. The events surrounding the fall of the nation are a down payment on a fuller judgment to come on all humanity. The presence of one guarantees the other.
With Jesus’ return comes the manifestation of judgment and final salvation (redemption).
verses.commentary:
21:28 "But when these things begin to take place" These prophecies of Mark 13, Matthew 24, and Luke 21
are meant to encourage

- those believers living between Jesus' death and the destruction of Jerusalem

- those believers who suffer persecution in every age (Idealism)

- those last generation Christians who will face the wrath of the Antichrist and his followers (Futurism)

- the events included in the Jewish war (A.D. 66-70, Partial Preterism)

▣ "straighten up and lift up your heads" These are both AORIST ACTIVE IMPERATIVES.
Believers' courage in the face of persecution and death is a powerful witness to the unbelievers who tremble in
fear (cf. Luke 21:25-26).

This may be OT imagery of

- the King of glory entering Jerusalem/temple with the righteous ‒ Psalm 24

- YHWH saving, protecting, and bringing His righteous people to Himself ‒ Psalm 118

- imagery of Jerusalem's strong wall but gates opened by God for the righteous ‒ Isaiah 26; Rev. 21:25

▣ "because your redemption is drawing near" Verses 29-36 are built on the promise of Luke 21:28. It
shows that Christians amid sufferings still have great confidence.

▣ "redemption" This means "purchased release" (found only here in the Gospels). It is the common
OT term for God's gracious acts toward His people.

Mark 13:28-32 is also in Luke 21:29-33.

verses.zh: 耶稣又设比喻对他们说：「你们看无花果树和各样的树；它发芽的时候，你们一看见，自然晓得夏天近了。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] he told them a parable: “Look at the fig tree and all the other trees.[NOTE:2]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “all the trees.”
verses.commentary:
21:29 "He told them a parable" This is also recorded in Matt. 24:32-35 and Mark 13:28-31. The little phrase
"and all the trees" is unique to Luke and widens the warning. Although believers cannot know
the specific time of Jesus' coming, they can know the general time (cf. Luke 21:30-31).

Special Topic: Parable Interpretation

verses.zh: a
verses.en: When they sprout leaves, you see[NOTE:1] for yourselves and know that summer is now near.
notes: Grk “seeing for yourselves, you know.” The participle βλέποντες (blepontes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

verses.zh: 这样，你们看见这些事渐渐地成就，也该晓得　神的国近了。
verses.en: So also you, when you see these things happening, know[NOTE:1] that the kingdom of God[NOTE:2] is near.
notes: The verb γινώσκετε (ginōskete, “know”) can be parsed as either present indicative or present imperative. In this context the imperative fits better, since the movement is from analogy (trees and seasons) to the future (the signs of the coming of the kingdom) and since the emphasis is on preparation for this event.
The kingdom of God refers here to the kingdom in all its power. See Luke 17:20-37.
verses.commentary:
21:31 "the kingdom of God" This refers to God's temporal coming in judgment on Jerusalem. This
understanding is possible because of the last phrase, "is near."

▣ "is near" Believers cannot know the exact time of Jesus' coming judgment on Jerusalem,
even He did not know (cf. Matt. 24:36). They will be surprised by it (cf. Matt. 24:44), but they can know the general
season (Matt. 24:32-35; Mark 13:28-31) and be prepared for it.

The concept of the soon return has been a problem for Dispensational interpreters because of the
2,000-year gap. They put gaps in several places in prophetic texts so as to fit their eschatological grid, but nothing
in the texts themselves warrant this (e.g., Daniel 2).

Special Topic: Soon Return

verses.zh: 我实在告诉你们，这世代还没有过去，这些事都要成就。
verses.en: I tell you the truth,[NOTE:1] this generation[NOTE:2] will not pass away until all these things take place.
notes: Grk “Truly (ἀμήν, amēn), I say to you.”

This is one of the hardest verses in the gospels to interpret. Various views exist for what generation means. (1) Some take it as meaning “race” and thus as an assurance that the Jewish race (nation) will not pass away. But it is very questionable that the Greek term γενεά (genea) can have this meaning. Two other options are possible. (2) Generation might mean “this type of generation” and refer to the generation of wicked humanity. Then the point is that humanity will not perish because God will redeem it. Or (3) generation may refer to “the generation that sees the signs of the end” (vv. 25-26), who will also see the end itself. In other words, once the movement to the return of Christ starts, all the events connected with it happen very quickly, in rapid succession.
verses.commentary:
21:32 "Truly I say to you" This is literally, "amen." It is parallel to the idiom found in Luke 21:3.

Special Topic: Amen

▣ "this generation will not pass away until all things take place" This is a strong
DOUBLE NEGATIVE. There has been much discussion about the interpretation of "this generation"
(cf. Matt. 11:16; 12:39,41,42,45; 16:4; 17:17; 23:36; 24:34; Mark 8:12,38; 9:19; 13:30; Luke 7:31; 9:41;
11:29,30,31,32,50,51; 17:25; 21:23). There are two major theories.

- this refers specifically to the Jewish War in A.D.
66-70, which culminated in the destruction of Jerusalem

- this phrase is used in its OT sense of a people group in Deut. 32:5,20

Both are true and both fit this context. However, for me, other texts and historical information from Josephus
strongly imply this is another time marker related to the soon coming of God's judgment on "those who pierced Him" (cf. Rev. 1:7).

verses.zh: 天地要废去，我的话却不能废去。」
verses.en: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.[NOTE:1]
notes: The words that Jesus predicts here will never pass away. They are more stable and lasting than creation itself. For this kind of image, see Isa 40:8; 55:10-11.
verses.commentary:
21:33 This is another strong DOUBLE NEGATIVE. It is a powerful affirmation of the eternality
of God's promises (cf. Isa. 40:8; 55:11) and is repeated in Luke 16:17 and Matt. 5:18. Believers can trust
these unconditional truths.

- God's word

- God's character

- God's promises

- God's Son

- God's presence

- God's purposes

Notice the emphasis of the similar wording of Matt. 5:18, which speaks of the fact that the OT has
now been superceded by the words of Jesus (cf. Luke 21:21-48)! Jesus is the Father's ultimate and complete revelation of
Himself (cf. John 1:1-18; Phil. 2:6-11; Col. 1:15-23; Heb. 1:2-3).

Special Topic: Covenant

verses.zh: 「你们要谨慎，恐怕因贪食、醉酒，并今生的思虑累住你们的心，那日子就如同网罗忽然临到你们；
verses.en: “But be on your guard[NOTE:1] so that your hearts are not weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and the worries of this life, and that day close down upon you suddenly like a trap.[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “watch out for yourselves.”sn Disciples are to watch out. If they are too absorbed into everyday life, they will stop watching and living faithfully.

Or like a thief, see Luke 12:39-40. The metaphor of a trap is a vivid one. Most modern English translations traditionally place the words “like a trap” at the end of v. 34, completing the metaphor. In the Greek text (and in the NRSV and REB) the words “like a trap” are placed at the beginning of v. 35. This does not affect the meaning.
verses.commentary:
21:34 "Be on guard" This is a PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVE. It is a recurrent warning
(cf. Luke 12:40,45 Mark 4:19; Matt. 24:42-44) and is the major thrust of Jesus' eschatological teachings:

- be ready

- be watching

- be active in My service

▣ "hearts" In this context "yourselves" and "hearts" are parallel.

Special Topic: The Heart

▣ "weighted down with dissipation and drunkenness and the worries of life" This is addressed to the
early Jewish believers. The Christian life is a tension-filled pilgrimage. Many believers have damaged their witness and
effective ministry by the temptations and cares of this age. Salvation is not the end of the struggle; sometimes
it is the beginning (i.e., Romans 7; Eph. 6:10-19).

The parallel of the soils in Mark 4 and Matthew 13 is a shocking witness to the need for fruit
bearing and perseverance, not just initial response (germination). Salvation is an ongoing relationship
(cf. Matt. 10:32; Mark 13:13), not a ticket to heaven or an insurance policy! Daily choices reveal the
heart and the true self. Faithfulness and perseverance are evidence of a free salvation.

Special Topic: The Need to Persevere

▣ "and that day will come on you suddenly like a trap" "That day" is an OT idiom for God's visitation
for blessing or judgment.

Special Topic: That Day

Special Topic: The Day of the Lord

verses.zh: 因为那日子要这样临到全地上一切居住的人。
verses.en: For[NOTE:1] it will overtake[NOTE:2] all who live on the face of the whole earth.[NOTE:3]
notes: There is debate in the textual tradition about the position of γάρ (gar) and whether v. 35 looks back to v. 34 or is independent. The textual evidence does slightly favor placing γάρ after the verb and thus linking it back to v. 34. The other reading looks like Isa 24:17. However, the construction is harsh and the translation prefers for stylistic reasons to start a new English sentence here.
Or “come upon.”
This judgment involves everyone: all who live on the face of the whole earth. No one will escape this evaluation.
verses.commentary:
21:35 This may be an allusion to Isa. 24:17 in the Septuagint. If so, then the verse division slightly
changes.

God's coming visitation ("that day," Luke 21:34) will impact all human beings living and dead
(i.e., 1 Thess. 4:13-18; Phil. 2:10-11). All will give an account to God of the gift of life (cf. Matt. 25:31-46; 2 Cor. 5:10; Rev. 20:11-15).

For those who know God in Christ, it is a day of resurrection, reunion, and rejoicing. But, for
those who have not responded to the gospel, it is a day of gloom, doom, rejection, and permanent judgment
(separation).

Special Topic: The Last Days

Special Topic: Eternal Punishment (hell)

▣ "those who dwell on the face of all the earth" Verse 36 seems to limit v. 35 in two ways.

- "earth" (gē) can refer to Palestine

Special Topic: Land, Country, Earth

- "all the things that are about to take place" ‒ This denotes the immediate hearers (i.e., Matt. 24:34). This is one of many
time indicators in the Olivet Discourse and the book of Revelation. Jesus' words are directed to that generation,
not 2,000+ years in the future!

▣ "and to stand before the Son of Man" At first glance this seems to relate to Matt. 24-25; Rev. 20, but as we
have seen, these texts (i.e., the literary unit of Matt. 23-25) refer to the Jewish war (A.D. 66-70).

verses.zh: 你们要时时警醒，常常祈求，使你们能逃避这一切要来的事，得以站立在人子面前。」
verses.en: But stay alert at all times,[NOTE:1] praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that must[NOTE:2] happen, and to stand before the Son of Man.”
notes: The call to be alert at all times is a call to remain faithful in looking for the Lord’s return.
For the translation of μέλλω (mellō) as “must,” see L&N 71.36.
verses.commentary:
21:36 "keep on the alert at all times" This is a PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVE denoting
constant attention (cf. Mark 13:33; Eph. 6:18). This verse reminds me of Eph. 6:19. There is a daily price
to be paid!

Paul uses a form of this term to describe his suffering for Christ and the gospel in 2 Cor. 6:5
and 11:27.

Special Topic: Spiritual Warfare

▣ "praying" This is a PRESENT MIDDLE (deponent) PARTICIPLE used in
the sense of an IMPERATIVE. Luke uses this term often in the sense of

- beseech or pray, Luke 5:12; 8:38; 10:2; 21:36; 22:32; Acts 4:31; 8:22,24; 10:2

- beg, Luke 8:28; 9:38,40; Acts 21:39; 26:3

- please tell, Acts 8:34

All of these senses are found in the Septuagint.

Special Topic: Effective Prayer

NASB, NRSV
"that you may have strength to escape"

NKJV
"that you may be counted worthy to escape"

TEV, REB
"that you will have the strength to go safely through"

NJB
"for the strength to survive"

Peshitta
"that you may be worthy to escape"

This is a purpose clause (hina) with an AORIST ACTIVE SUBJUNCTIVE
(a note of contingency) and an AORIST ACTIVE INFINITIVE. Some believers will be caught unaware
and unprepared when the events of the coming siege of Jerusalem rapidly unfold.

There is a Greek manuscript variant in this phrase.

- kataxiōthēte (AORIST PASSIVE SUBJUNCTIVE), "may be judged/counted worthy"
(cf. MSS A, C, D; Peshitta, NKJV)

- katischusēte (AORIST ACTIVE SUBJUNCTIVE), "may have strength"
(cf. MSS א, B, L, W and in UBS4; NASB, TEV, REB, NJB)

verses.zh: 耶稣每日在殿里教训人，每夜出城在一座山，名叫橄榄山住宿。
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] every day Jesus[NOTE:2] was teaching in the temple courts,[NOTE:3] but at night he went and stayed[NOTE:4] on the Mount of Olives.[NOTE:5]
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” since vv. 37-38 serve as something of a summary or transition from the discourse preceding to the passion narrative that follows.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “in the temple.”
Grk “and spent the night,” but this is redundant because of the previous use of the word “night.”
See the note on the phrase Mount of Olives in 19:29.tn Grk “at the mountain called ‘of Olives.’”
verses.commentary:
21:37 "during the day He was teaching in the temple" Jesus did not hide or decrease His public ministry
(cf. Luke 20:1). These regular teaching sessions took place at Solomon's Portico.

▣ "spend the night on the mount that is called Olivet" This refers to the fact that Jesus camped
out on the Mount of Olives several nights and did not spend every night with Mary, Martha, and Lazarus in Bethany.
This place was well known to Judas and will be the site of Jesus' arrest.

Special Topic: Gethsemane

verses.zh: 众百姓清早上圣殿，到耶稣那里，要听他讲道。
verses.en: And all the people[NOTE:1] came to him early in the morning to listen to him in the temple courts.[NOTE:2]
notes: Jesus’ teaching was still quite popular with all the people at this point despite the leaders’ opposition.
Some mss (those of ƒ13) place John 7:53-8:11 here after v. 38, no doubt because it was felt that this was a better setting for the pericope.tn Grk “in the temple.”

gr.gloss: would come early in the morning

verses.commentary:
21:38 This shows Jesus' popularity with both the pilgrims attending the Passover and the local townspeople.
This popularity was one of several reasons that caused the religious leaders to fear Him.

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You,

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- What spiritual truth about stewardship was Jesus communicating in Luke 21:1-4?

- Why were the Jews so proud of the temple?

- Why is the discussion of the destruction of Jerusalem mixed with end-time events of the End of the Age?

- What does the phrase in verse 25, "the times of the Gentiles," mean?

- What is the major emphasis of Jesus' teachings concerning His Second Coming?

- Do Luke 21:34-36 refer to believers? If so what is the implication?
